newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian court ruling on SS officer revives trauma.
newsitem.headline: Italian court ruling on SS officer revives trauma.

text.p: A decision by Italy's highest appeal court to order a re-trial of former SS captain Erich Priebke for his involvement in a World War Two massacre has revived controversy over a case which has come to haunt the country.

The Court of Cassation on Tuesday annulled a bitterly contested August 1 verdict at Priebke's first trial which found him guilty of multiple murder but freed him because of mitigating circumstances and a statute of limitations.
Relatives of the 335 men and boys who died in the 1944 Nazi atrocity welcomed the news, but one of the three judges who presided over the initial trial lashed out at the ruling.
"They are doing all they can to make sure that Priebke dies in prison," said military judge Bruno Rocchi.
Priebke, 83, has been held in a central Rome jail since the August verdict awaiting the outcome of the appeals and a German extradition order.

Antonino Intelisano, the Italian lawyer who prosecuted Priebke in the military tribunal, said the German's extradition request would now have to wait, but added that the authorities would review the question of whether Priebke should stay in jail.
Priebke's lawyer Velio di Rezzo blasted Tuesday's high court ruling as "absolutely unjust" and said he planned to demand that his client be released into house arrest.
Priebke went on trial amidst a blaze of publicity on May 8, accused of complicity over the infamous massacre at the Ardeatine Caves south of Rome in March 1944.
The chaotic proceedings, which at times bordered on farce, ended in a 2-1 verdict ruling that while Priebke had taken part in the killings he could not be jailed.
The convoluted ruling drew worldwide condemnation, while leading Italian politicians openly questioned the decision.

The high court squashed the verdict by overturning a lower appeal court's decision from July which rejected accusations that the presiding judge in the case, Agostino Quistelli, was biased in favour of the accused.

"This is the redemption of the Italian justice system," said Shimon Samuels, director of international affairs for the Los Angeles-based Simon Wiesenthal Center, which tracks former Nazis and closely followed the Priebke case.
Samuels said Intelisano had indicated the trial might be held within three or four months, but judge Rocchi said there would be problems choosing a new panel to hear the case.
"After everything that has happened, I think only a madman would agree to be a judge," he said.
The Ardeatine Caves massacre took place in reprisal for a partisan bomb attack on German soldiers in Rome.

Priebke, who lived openly for almost 50 years in Argentina before being brought to Italy for trial, admitted shooting two people and checking off names from a list at the caves, but his lawyers argued he should not be held responsible because he had to follow orders.
